{{unfocused |date=May 2024}}
In [[Abstract_algebra|algebra]], the term '''Hermite ring''' (after [[Charles Hermite]]) has been applied to three different objects.

According to [[Irving Kaplansky|Kaplansky]] (1949),<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Kaplansky |first=Irving |date=July 1949 |title=Elementary Divisors and Modules |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1990591?origin=crossref |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=66 |issue=2 |pages=464 |doi=10.2307/1990591|url-access=subscription }}</ref> a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] is '''right Hermite''' if, for every two elements ''a'' and ''b'' of the ring, there is an element ''d'' of the ring and an [[invertible matrix|invertible]] 2×2 [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] ''M'' over the ring such that (''a'' ''b'')''M'' = (''d'' 0), and the term '''left Hermite''' is defined similarly.  Matrices over such a ring can be put in [[Hermite normal form]] by right multiplication by a [[square matrix|square]] invertible matrix.<ref name=":0" />  [[Tsit Yuen Lam|Lam]] (2006)<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Lam |first=Tsit Yuen |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-540-34575-6 |title=Serre’s Problem on Projective Modules |date=2006 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-23317-6 |series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-34575-6}}</ref> calls this property '''K-Hermite''', using ''Hermite'' instead in the sense given below.

According to Lam (1978),<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Lam |first=T. Y. |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BFb0068340 |title=Serre’s Conjecture |date=1978 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-08657-4 |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=635 |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/bfb0068340}}</ref> a ring is '''right Hermite''' if any finitely generated [[stably free module|stably free]] right [[module (mathematics)|module]] over the ring is [[free module|free]]. This is equivalent to requiring that any row vector (''b''<sub>1</sub>,...,''b<sub>n</sub>'') of elements of the ring which generate it as a right module (i.e., ''b''<sub>1</sub>''R'' + ... + ''b<sub>n</sub>R'' = ''R'') can be completed to a (not necessarily square{{clarify|date=September 2023}}) invertible matrix by adding some number of rows. The criterion of being '''left Hermite''' can be defined similarly. Lissner (1965)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lissner |first=David |date=April 1965 |title=Outer Product Rings |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1994132?origin=crossref |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=116 |pages=526 |doi=10.2307/1994132}}</ref> earlier called a [[commutative ring]] with this property an '''H-ring'''.

According to [[Paul Cohn|Cohn]] (2006),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cohn |first=Paul Moritz |title=Free ideal rings and localization in general rings |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge university press |isbn=978-0-521-85337-8 |series=New mathematical monographs |location=Cambridge (GB)}}</ref> a ring is '''Hermite''' if, in addition to every stably free (left) module being free, it has [[invariant basis number]].

All commutative rings which are Hermite in the sense of Kaplansky are also Hermite in the sense of Lam, but the [[converse (logic)|converse]] is not necessarily true.  All [[Bézout domain]]s are Hermite in the sense of Kaplansky, and a commutative ring which is Hermite in the sense of Kaplansky is also a [[Bézout ring]].<ref name=":1" />

The '''Hermite ring conjecture''', introduced by Lam (1978),<ref name=":2" /> states that if ''R'' is a commutative Hermite ring, then the [[polynomial ring]] ''R''[''x''] is also a Hermite ring.
